title: AI music & sound
content_html:
What We're Doing

In this session, learners explore how artificial intelligence can generate original music, beats, and soundtracks from simple text descriptions or musical prompts. Students will experiment with AI music generation tools to create short soundtracks for imaginary scenes (like a movie trailer, a game level, or a walk through Nairobi), and beats they could imagine using in a song. Along the way, they'll discover how AI "listens" to patterns in existing music to create something new, and they'll think critically about creativity, originality, and authorship when a machine makes art.

By the end of the lesson, each student will have generated at least one original piece of AI music/audio, given it a title and a purpose (e.g., "battle music for a video game"), and reflected on how the AI interpreted their instructions.

Tools & Resources

  • Suno AI (https://suno.com) — Generates full songs with vocals and instruments from text prompts. Free tier: limited number of generations per day (varies, typically ~10-50 credits/day); requires an account (email or Google sign-in).
  • Soundraw (https://soundraw.io) — Generates instrumental beats/soundtracks by mood, genre, and length. Free tier allows preview/creation but often restricts full-quality downloads without a paid plan.
  • Boomy (https://boomy.com) — Beginner-friendly AI song creation with simple style selection. Free tier allows song creation and limited saves; publishing/downloading may require payment.
  • AIVA (https://www.aiva.ai) — Good for instrumental/orchestral soundtrack style music. Free tier has monthly download limits and usage restrictions for commercial use.
  • Backup option (offline-friendly): Pre-downloaded sample tracks/screenshots from the above tools in case of poor internet connectivity — prepare at least 3 examples in advance.
  • Headphones or speakers for listening (shared or personal, depending on classroom setup).

Note: Most of these tools require an internet connection and may need an email sign-up. Check data/bandwidth availability beforehand and consider using a single shared classroom account if individual sign-ups aren't practical.

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. Begin with a 5-minute discussion: Ask "Where have you heard music or sound made by a computer before?" (game music, ringtones, ads). Explain that today they will make their own AI-generated music.
  2. Show a live demo: open Soundraw or Boomy and generate one track using the prompt style "upbeat, hopeful, hip-hop, 30 seconds" — play it for the class.
  3. Explain the concept simply: "The AI has learned patterns from thousands of songs — rhythms, chords, and instruments that usually go together. When you give it a mood or genre, it recombines those patterns to create something new."
  4. Assign or let students choose a theme for their soundtrack, e.g., "music for exploring a jungle," "beats for a superhero," or "calm music for studying."
  5. Have students open their assigned tool (Soundraw, Boomy, or AIVA) and select a mood/genre matching their theme.
  6. Guide them to generate at least 2 versions of their track by changing one variable each time (e.g., tempo, mood, or instrument) — this shows how input changes affect the AI's output.
  7. Ask students to name their final track and write one sentence describing where/how it would be used (e.g., "Fast Feet — background music for a running game").
  8. If using Suno, guide advanced students to try adding lyrics with a prompt like: "Write an upbeat Afrobeat song about friendship in Nairobi" — and generate the result.
  9. Have each student (or pair) play their favourite generated track to the class (30 seconds max per group to manage time).
  10. Close with a group reflection: "What surprised you about what the AI created?"

Example Outputs

  • "Jungle Steps" — A 45-second instrumental track generated with the prompt "adventurous, tribal drums, jungle theme" on Soundraw, meant to accompany an imaginary explorer game level.
  • "Nairobi Nights" — A Boomy-generated Afrobeat/pop instrumental with a moderate tempo, described by the student as "music for a matatu ride through the city at night."
  • "Friendship Anthem" — A full song with AI-generated vocals from Suno using the prompt "Afrobeat song about friendship, happy mood," complete with a simple chorus the student found funny and shared with the class.

Facilitation Tips

  • Pre-test tools beforehand: Confirm the free tier is working and check daily generation limits before class — some tools reset limits at unpredictable times.
  • Prepare backups: Save 3–5 pre-generated tracks/screenshots in case internet is slow or a tool is down.
  • Manage generation time: AI music generation can take 30 seconds to 2 minutes per track — use this waiting time to have students write their track description or brainstorm the next variation.
  • Headphone logistics: If students don't have headphones, pair them up or use short "listening rounds" where the whole class listens to one track at a time through speakers.
  • Handle weird outputs calmly: AI-generated lyrics or music can sometimes be nonsensical, repetitive, or unexpected — treat this as a teaching moment about AI limitations rather than an error to fix.
  • Group size: If accounts/devices are limited, work in pairs or small groups of 3 so everyone gets hands-on time.
  • Watch the clock: Cap final track-sharing to 30 seconds per student/group to keep the whole class engaged and finish on time.

Discussion Questions

  • How do you think the AI "knows" what a happy or sad song sounds like?
  • What is the difference between a human composer and an AI generating music — do they create in the same way?
  • If an AI makes a song, who owns it — you, the AI, or the company that built the tool?
  • Did the AI create exactly what you imagined, or something different? Why do you think that happened?
  • Should AI-generated music be allowed in movies, adverts, or the radio? Why or why not?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Generate two versions of the same theme by changing only the mood (e.g., "happy" vs "mysterious") and compare how different the results sound.
  • Medium: Create a 3-track "mini soundtrack" for a short story or scene with a beginning, middle, and end (e.g., calm intro, tense middle, triumphant ending), and explain your prompt choices for each.
  • Hard: Combine an AI-generated beat with a recorded voice or clap rhythm (using a phone recorder) to create a short "remix," and present how you merged human and AI elements together.
